chapter_title: The Decorator Pattern: Enhancing Objects Dynamically

screens.title: The Decorator Pattern: Enhancing Objects Dynamically
screens.subtitle: Add responsibilities to objects at runtime without changing their class.

narration.text: In this short orientation we’ll frame why the Decorator pattern matters and how you will use it. The fundamental claim is simple: instead of creating many subclasses to cover every feature combination, you compose small decorator objects around a base object at runtime. This approach keeps the base class unchanged, supports flexible combinations, and adheres to principles like Open/Closed and Single Responsibility. You will see a concrete coffee example and a notification exercise where SMS, Email and Logging decorators are combined. The pattern depends on a common component interface so the client code interacts only with the contract, not the concrete layers. That uniformity makes decorated objects transparent and composable. We will also compare Decorator to inheritance and point out common pitfalls such as too many layers or decorators that do too much. By the end of the chapter you will be able to implement simple decorators in C#, compose them at runtime, and decide when Decorator is the right tool. Think of this as learning to assemble features like toppings on a coffee rather than baking a new cake for every flavor combination.

keyIdea.text: Decorator composes behaviors at runtime so you avoid subclass explosion and keep classes focused.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Four practical goals for using Decorator effectively

narration.text: These objectives map what you should be able to do after working through the chapter. First, you will be able to explain the purpose of the Decorator pattern: to add responsibilities to objects dynamically and transparently so clients need not be aware of decoration layers. Second, you should be able to contrast Decorator with subclassing and identify when composition is preferable to inheritance to avoid class explosion. Third, you will implement a Decorator in C#—defining the component interface, a concrete component, an abstract decorator, and concrete decorators—and compose them at runtime. Fourth, you will recognize scenarios where decorators fit best and also spot common mistakes, such as creating decorators that violate single responsibility or introducing performance issues through many layers. Each objective focuses on a practical competency: explanation, comparison, implementation, and judgement. These skills let you design modular features that are easy to combine, test, and maintain, which is why the Decorator pattern is a useful tool in production systems.

screens.title: What the Decorator pattern is
screens.subtitle: A structural pattern for dynamic, transparent extension

narration.text: The Decorator pattern is a structural pattern that adds responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it with decorator objects that share the same interface. In plain terms, you give a component a standard contract, and both the base object and each decorator implement that contract so they can substitute for one another. This is important because it means clients call the same operations whether they receive a raw object or a multi-layered decorated object. A clear example is a coffee object with methods for description and cost. A milk decorator wraps the coffee, calling the wrapped object's methods but adding its own contribution. This keeps each class focused: the base object has core behavior and each decorator adds a single responsibility. A common misconception is that decorators are simply a variant of inheritance. In fact they are composition-based and avoid creating one subclass per feature combination. Another misconception is that decorators must be immutable; they can hold state if needed but that state should not violate the component contract. A final practical note: ensure decorators respect the interface contract and do not change expectations, or the chain will break client assumptions. What matters is transparency and single responsibility in each decorator.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Decorator wraps objects that implement the same interface, adding behavior while remaining interchangeable.

content.html:
Core Concept
Decorator pattern — definition
A composition-based approach to add responsibilities to objects dynamically while preserving a uniform interface for clients.
Key properties
  • Uses a common component interface.
  • Concrete decorators wrap a component and enhance behavior.
  • Supports runtime combinations without new subclasses.
Concrete example (conceptual)
A SimpleCoffee implements ICoffee. A MilkDecorator implements ICoffee and holds an ICoffee reference. MilkDecorator adds cost and description while delegating other calls.
Analogy: Coffee order
Start with a base coffee. Add milk, sugar, caramel in any order. Each topping decorates the base and changes taste and cost. No need for a specific subclass for every topping combination.
Key Takeaway
Decorator favors composition over inheritance to keep behavior modular and combinable at runtime.

screens.title: Coffee example: building decorators step by step
screens.subtitle: From SimpleCoffee to a decorated order

narration.text: Let's walk through a simple step-by-step process of creating and composing decorators using the coffee example. Step one is to define the component interface with the operations clients need, for example methods that return description and cost. Step two is to create the concrete component that implements that interface, such as SimpleCoffee with base cost and description. Step three is to implement an abstract decorator that also implements the component interface and maintains a reference to another component; by default it delegates calls to the wrapped component. Step four is to implement concrete decorators like MilkDecorator and SugarDecorator that override delegated methods to add behavior before or after delegating. Step five is composition: at runtime you wrap a SimpleCoffee with one or more decorators in any order to assemble the final object and then call methods through the interface. A common runtime check is to print description and observe incremental changes, and to compute aggregated cost. A misconception is assuming the order never matters; in some cases order changes results, so test chains. Practically, unit tests that exercise combinations will reveal ordering or state-related problems before production.

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Define interface → concrete component → abstract decorator → concrete decorators → compose at runtime.

content.html:
Process Flow
Step-by-step: Coffee decorators
1
Define component interface
Operations: GetDescription(), GetCost(). Clients program to this interface only.
2
Create concrete component
SimpleCoffee implements the interface and returns base values.
3
Implement abstract decorator
Implements the interface and holds an inner component reference, delegating by default.
4
Create concrete decorators
MilkDecorator adds cost and description, calling the wrapped component's methods then adding its contribution.
5
Compose at runtime
Wrap the base with decorators as needed and call the interface methods to get combined behavior.
Concrete example
Compose: new SugarDecorator(new MilkDecorator(new SimpleCoffee())). Calling GetDescription returns a concatenated description that reflects each decorator's addition. GetCost returns the sum of each cost contribution.
Common misconception
Assuming decorators are identical to subclasses. They are composition wrappers and allow runtime assembly rather than compile-time subclassing.
Key Takeaway

Follow the five steps to structure decorator code and test composed chains to verify behavior and order sensitivity.

screens.title: Core components and their relationships
screens.subtitle: Component interface, concrete component, abstract decorator, concrete decorators

narration.text: Understanding the relationship among the core parts of the Decorator pattern clarifies how composition works. The Component interface is the contract both the concrete component and decorators implement; it assures the client can call operations uniformly. The Concrete Component provides core, unadorned behavior — for example SimpleCoffee returns a base description and cost. The Abstract Decorator also implements the Component interface and holds a reference to another Component. Its default behavior is to delegate to the wrapped component, which makes it a transparent pass-through unless overridden. Concrete Decorators inherit from the abstract decorator and add a single responsibility such as appending a description fragment or adding to the cost. The hierarchy is not an inheritance explosion but a thin abstraction that enables runtime wrapping. Be careful when decorators depend on wrapped state or when they alter method contracts; they must preserve the Component interface semantics to avoid breaking clients. This hierarchy supports nesting arbitrarily deep, but code clarity and performance should guide how many layers you actually use in practice. Core components and their relationships means a uniform interface plus a thin abstract decorator layer enables safe, nested composition of behaviors.. In practical terms, component interface, concrete component, abstract decorator, concrete decorators. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Relationships
keyIdea.text: A uniform interface plus a thin abstract decorator layer enables safe, nested composition of behaviors.

content.html:
Structure
Pattern hierarchy
Component interface → Concrete Component; Abstract Decorator → Concrete Decorators. The abstract decorator holds and delegates to a Component reference.
Component Interface
Defines contract (e.g., GetDescription, GetCost). Both components and decorators implement it.
Abstract Decorator
Implements the interface and stores a reference to a Component. Delegates by default to the wrapped object.
Annotation cards
Concrete Component
Provides base behavior. Example: SimpleCoffee returns "Simple Coffee" and base cost.
Concrete Decorator
Overrides methods to add to description or cost, while delegating other calls to the wrapped component.
Pro tip
Keep each decorator focused on a single responsibility. If it grows complex, consider splitting it into multiple decorators or refactoring responsibilities elsewhere.
Key Takeaway

The abstract decorator is the thin wrapper that makes transparent, stackable composition possible while preserving client expectations.

screens.title: C#: ICoffee and SimpleCoffee implementation
screens.subtitle: Interface and the concrete component example

narration.text: Now we will look at concrete C# code for the component and a simple concrete component to ground the pattern. The component interface declares the operations that are uniform across the chain; in the coffee example these are GetDescription and GetCost. The SimpleCoffee class implements this interface and returns a base description and base cost. When you implement the interface in C#, keep method semantics stable—decorators will rely on these return values to build their additions. This is a minimal, testable unit: you can write a test that asserts SimpleCoffee returns "Simple Coffee" and cost 5.0. A common mistake is embedding side effects or input and output in the base component that decorators also repeat; keep the base behavior focused so decorations cleanly add responsibility. The code snippet shown is ready to be wrapped by decorators in subsequent steps, and it is intentionally small so you can see how decorators layer on top without changing the original class. keyIdea.text: Define a small interface and a focused concrete component so decorators can augment behavior transparently.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
ICoffee & SimpleCoffee
Interface and a simple concrete component implementing description and cost.
using System;

// Component Interface
public interface ICoffee
{
  string GetDescription();
  double GetCost();
}

// Concrete Component
public class SimpleCoffee : ICoffee
{
  public string GetDescription()
  {
    return "Simple Coffee";
  }

  public double GetCost()
  {
    return 5.0; // Base cost
  }
}
Run the simple class in a test to confirm the base behavior. Decorators will wrap instances of ICoffee and extend these methods.
Example output to expect
Description: Simple Coffee; Cost: $5.0. You can assert these expectations in unit tests before adding decorators.
Why keep it small?
A focused concrete component makes decorator behavior easier to reason about and test. Avoid side effects in core methods that decorators must replicate.

screens.title: C#: CoffeeDecorator and concrete decorators
screens.subtitle: Abstract decorator and Milk, Sugar, Caramel examples

narration.text: Next we'll examine the abstract decorator and a few concrete decorators in C#. The abstract decorator implements the component interface and holds a reference to another component. Its methods typically delegate calls to the wrapped component so that concrete decorators can override behavior selectively. For example, a MilkDecorator overrides GetDescription to append ", with Milk" to the wrapped component's description and overrides GetCost to add a fixed milk surcharge. Similarly, SugarDecorator and CaramelDecorator add their own description fragments and costs. When you implement these, make sure constructors accept an ICoffee to wrap and that overridden methods call the wrapped object's methods where appropriate. That delegation keeps the chain intact and allows decorators to be stacked. A practical test is to wrap a SimpleCoffee first with MilkDecorator and then with SugarDecorator, then verify that description concatenates both additions and the cost sums the contributions. Remember to avoid decorators that both mutate internal state and return inconsistent results; prefer functional additions where possible to keep behavior predictable. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decorator code
keyIdea.text: Abstract decorator delegates to wrapped component; concrete decorators add small, focused changes to description and cost.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
CoffeeDecorator & Concrete Decorators
public abstract class CoffeeDecorator : ICoffee
{
  protected ICoffee _decoratedCoffee;

  public CoffeeDecorator(ICoffee coffee)
  {
    _decoratedCoffee = coffee;
  }

  public virtual string GetDescription()
  {
    return _decoratedCoffee.GetDescription();
  }

  public virtual double GetCost()
  {
    return _decoratedCoffee.GetCost();
  }
}

public class MilkDecorator : CoffeeDecorator
{
  public MilkDecorator(ICoffee coffee) : base(coffee) { }

  public override string GetDescription()
  {
    return _decoratedCoffee.GetDescription() + ", with Milk";
  }

  public override double GetCost()
  {
    return _decoratedCoffee.GetCost() + 1.5;
  }
}
Testing the chain
Compose: var coffee = new SugarDecorator(new MilkDecorator(new SimpleCoffee())); Verify the description includes both toppings and the cost is the sum of base and toppings.
Common pitfall
Avoid decorators that perform unrelated responsibilities or that change return semantics expected by the interface; keep each decorator focused and predictable.

screens.title: Composing decorators at runtime
screens.subtitle: How wrapping orders and chains affect behavior

narration.text: Composition at runtime is the central benefit of the Decorator pattern, but it brings an important practical concern: the order of wrapping can affect results. When you chain decorators, each layer sees the results from the ones it wraps. That means adding milk then sugar may produce the same additive cost as sugar then milk, but in other domains the order can change data flow, formatting, or preconditions. For example, if one decorator compresses data and another encrypts it, encrypting before compressing usually yields poorer compression ratios. In the coffee example the order only affects description string concatenation, which is mostly harmless. Always think about whether decorators are commutative for your case. Testing multiple chains is essential. Another runtime consideration is performance: each decorator adds an indirection layer. For light UI features this overhead is negligible, but for hot inner loops you might prefer fewer layers or inline alternatives. Instrument or profile decorated chains if performance matters. Finally, document expected ordering and preconditions so future maintainers don't introduce incompatible decorators. Composing decorators at runtime means decorator order can matter; test combinations and profile for performance-sensitive code paths.. In practical terms, how wrapping orders and chains affect behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Composition notes
keyIdea.text: Decorator order can matter; test combinations and profile for performance-sensitive code paths.

content.html:
Runtime Composition
Compose and reason about order
Each decorator receives the wrapped object's output and may modify it. Order therefore influences behavior for non-commutative operations.
Example: Coffee order
Milk then Sugar yields description "Simple Coffee, with Milk, with Sugar". Costs add in any order. String concatenation is order-sensitive but harmless here.
Example: Data chain
Compression then encryption differs from encryption then compression. These operations are not commutative and order impacts correctness and efficiency.
Practical checks
  • Write tests for representative chains.
  • Document decorator preconditions and ordering rules.
  • Profile chains if used in performance-critical code paths.
Check your understanding
Name a pair of operations where order matters and explain why. Consider compression, encryption, formatting, and logging as candidates.
Key Takeaway

Think beyond composition: ordering and preconditions can change correctness and performance. Test the chains you create.

screens.title: Decorator vs Inheritance
screens.subtitle: Why composition often beats subclass explosion

narration.text: Comparing Decorator with inheritance clarifies when to use each technique. Inheritance encodes behavior combinations at compile time by creating subclasses. If you have many optional features, inheritance leads to a combinatorial explosion of classes such as MilkCoffee, SugarCoffee, MilkSugarCoffee, and so on. That approach is rigid and violates the Open/Closed Principle because adding a new feature often requires modifying the hierarchy or adding many combinations. The Decorator pattern instead composes small decorators at runtime so you can assemble only the features you need. Decorator supports Single Responsibility by giving each decorator a focused task. However, inheritance still has a place: if variants are fixed and well-defined, or when language constraints make runtime composition awkward, inheritance may be simpler. Performance can also favor inheritance in tight loops because there is no indirection. A useful heuristic is to prefer Decorator when the number of feature combinations is large or unknown, and prefer inheritance for a small, stable set of variants. Always balance clarity, maintainability, and performance when choosing a strategy. Decorator vs Inheritance means use decorator to avoid class explosion; use inheritance for small, stable variant sets with simple performance needs.. In practical terms, why composition often beats subclass explosion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Comparison
keyIdea.text: Use Decorator to avoid class explosion; use inheritance for small, stable variant sets with simple performance needs.

content.html:
Comparison
Decorator vs Inheritance
Inheritance
Compile-time variants, simple dispatch, but class explosion for many optional features.
Decorator
Runtime composition, flexible combinations, adheres to Open/Closed and Single Responsibility principles.
Heuristic
Prefer Decorator for many optional features. Prefer inheritance when variants are small, fixed, and performance-critical.
Concrete trade-offs
  • Decorator: flexible but adds indirection layers.
  • Inheritance: efficient dispatch but brittle hierarchy.
  • Consider testability, extensibility, and runtime needs.
Key Takeaway

Choose composition when flexibility matters; choose inheritance when variations are few and performance is paramount.

screens.title: Pitfalls and anti-patterns when using Decorator
screens.subtitle: Overuse, order mistakes, and violating interface expectations

narration.text: The Decorator pattern can be misused. A common pitfall is over-decorating: creating many layers where a simpler design or a single composite object would be clearer. Each decorator adds indirection, which can complicate debugging. Another mistake is making decorators do too much; a decorator should add one distinct responsibility. If it accumulates multiple responsibilities it becomes hard to reuse and test. Order sensitivity is another source of bugs—decorators that assume a specific precondition from an earlier layer can silently fail if applied in a different sequence. A related issue is changing the expected semantics of the interface: if a decorator alters return types, side effects, or error conditions outside what's specified by the component interface, clients can be surprised. To avoid these traps, document decorator contracts, write unit tests for representative chains, and prefer small, single-purpose decorators. If you need many features tightly coupled, consider refactoring into a composite or a different pattern that better matches requirements. Pitfalls and anti-patterns when using Decorator means avoid too many layers, multi-responsibility decorators, and undocumented ordering assumptions.. In practical terms, overuse, order mistakes, and violating interface expectations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls
keyIdea.text: Avoid too many layers, multi-responsibility decorators, and undocumented ordering assumptions.

content.html:
Common Mistakes
Anti-patterns to watch for
Overuse
Many tiny decorators can make debugging and comprehension difficult. Balance modularity with clarity.
Multi-responsibility
Decorators should avoid accumulating unrelated tasks; keep them single-purpose.
Order assumptions
If decorators expect particular input from earlier layers, document and test the required order.
Mitigation checklist
  • Write chain tests.
  • Document ordering constraints.
  • Limit decorator responsibilities.
Key Takeaway

Use small, well-documented decorators and ensure representative tests validate composed behavior and ordering rules.

screens.title: Notification system exercise and starter code
screens.subtitle: INotificationService, BaseNotification, NotificationDecorator, Sms and Email decorators

narration.text: The hands-on activity in the chapter asks you to implement a notification system using the Decorator pattern. Start by defining an INotificationService interface with a Send(string message) method. Implement BaseNotification that prints a basic message to the console. Then create an abstract NotificationDecorator that implements INotificationService and holds a wrapped INotificationService reference, delegating the Send call by default. Implement SmsDecorator and EmailDecorator as concrete decorators; each should call the wrapped service's Send method and then perform its own action like printing "Sending SMS:..." or "Sending Email:...". Chain decorators to create combined behaviors such as new SmsDecorator(new EmailDecorator(new BaseNotification())). Running this chain should show the base notification and then the additional messages from SMS and Email decorators. This exercise practices constructor injection, delegation, and observing combined side effects. Remember to remove the NotImplementedException in starter code and replace it with concrete email logic that calls base. Send(message) then prints the decorator-specific message so the entire chain runs as expected. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Notification decorator starter code
using System;

// 1. Component Interface
public interface INotificationService
{
  void Send(string message);
}

// 2. Concrete Component
public class BaseNotification : INotificationService
{
  public void Send(string message)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Base Notification: {message}");
  }
}

// 3. Abstract Decorator
public abstract class NotificationDecorator : INotificationService
{
  protected INotificationService _notificationService;

  public NotificationDecorator(INotificationService notificationService)
  {
    _notificationService = notificationService;
  }

  public virtual void Send(string message)
  {
    _notificationService.Send(message);
  }
}
Starter hints
  • Implement SmsDecorator and EmailDecorator to call base.Send then print their own message.
  • Chain decorators in Main to observe combined output.
  • Remove NotImplementedException in the sample Email method and replace with concrete logic.
Key Takeaway

Use this exercise to practice delegation, constructor injection, and verifying decorator chain side effects via console output or unit tests.

screens.title: Assessment question: DataProcessor example
screens.subtitle: Why choose Decorator over inheritance for optional, combinable features?

narration.text: Consider the assessment scenario: you have a DataProcessor class that processes byte arrays and you need optional features like logging, compression, and encryption that can be combined in any order. Would you use inheritance or the Decorator pattern? The correct answer is the Decorator pattern. Inheritance would require a separate subclass for every combination of features leading to a combinatorial explosion of classes, and it violates the Open/Closed Principle because adding a new feature forces changes to the class hierarchy. The Decorator pattern provides flexible, runtime composition: you define an IDataProcessor interface, keep the core DataProcessor as the concrete component, and implement LoggingDecorator, CompressionDecorator, and EncryptionDecorator that each wrap an IDataProcessor. Clients then compose chains like new LoggingDecorator(new EncryptionDecorator(new DataProcessor())). This approach avoids class explosion, keeps each decorator focused on one responsibility, and keeps the base class closed for modification yet open for extension. A common misconception is thinking decorators will reduce performance; while they add indirection, the design benefits and runtime flexibility usually outweigh the small overhead. For performance-critical inner loops evaluate and profile the decorator chain. Assessment question: DataProcessor example means decorator avoids class explosion and follows open/closed by composing optional features at runtime.. In practical terms, why choose decorator over inheritance for optional, combinable features?. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Justification bullets
  • Avoid class explosion when features combine arbitrarily.
  • Keep each feature as a separate, testable decorator.
  • Compose at runtime using constructor injection and wrapping.
Practical example
new LoggingDecorator(new EncryptionDecorator(new DataProcessor())). This composes logging and encryption without new subclasses for every combination.
Key Takeaway

When features are optional and combinable, implement each as a decorator to compose behavior cleanly at runtime.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember about the Decorator pattern

narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to remember. First, the Decorator pattern lets you add responsibilities to objects dynamically by wrapping them in decorators that share the same component interface. Second, the abstract decorator is a thin layer that delegates to a wrapped component, enabling transparency and nested composition. Third, decorators should be single-purpose and composable; avoid multi-responsibility decorators and document ordering. Keep unit tests that exercise representative decorator chains to catch ordering and contract issues early. Use Decorator to avoid a class explosion when many optional features exist, but prefer inheritance when variants are few, fixed, and performance is critical. Finally, always ensure decorators preserve the component interface semantics so client expectations remain valid. These points will help you design maintainable, extensible systems that add behavior without modifying existing classes.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Decorator composes behavior at runtime; keep decorators focused and test chains for ordering.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Quick reference cards for implementation and judgement

narration.text: These three compact reminders will guide implementation and architectural decisions. First, implement a small component interface and a focused concrete component so decorators can augment behavior safely. Second, make the abstract decorator delegate by default and have concrete decorators override only the parts they extend, keeping responsibilities narrow. Third, test composed chains and document ordering rules; this prevents surprises where decorators interact badly. When deciding between Decorator and inheritance, weigh the number of feature combinations, clarity, and performance. Decorator shines for many optional features and runtime flexibility. Keep decorators small, test chains thoroughly, and profile when performance is critical. These habits will help you use the Decorator pattern to build maintainable and extensible systems without unnecessary subclasses. Small interface
Keep operations focused and stable so decorators can compose safely.
Delegate default behavior
Abstract decorator should forward calls so concrete decorators override only what they must.
Test and document
Exercise representative chains and specify ordering constraints to avoid surprises.
Final takeaway

Decorator is a practical, composition-based way to extend objects dynamically. Use it when flexibility and clean separation of responsibilities matter.
